@fileOperations.button.cancel.description: Button that closes a copy/move/delete/new-file/new-folder dialog without taking the action. Short control label.

@fileOperations.button.close.description: Replaces Cancel in the new-folder and new-file dialogs while a slow create is still running: it closes the dialog but does NOT stop the create, which is why it isn't 'Cancel'. Short control label.

@fileOperations.button.ok.description: Confirm button in the new-file and new-folder dialogs. Short control label; this is the affirmative OK, not a status word.

@fileOperations.delete.fromPath.description: Header line in the delete-confirm dialog showing the folder the items are deleted from. The path is abbreviated (home shown as ~).

@fileOperations.delete.noTrashWarningStr.description: Bold lead of a warning banner in the delete dialog, shown on volumes (FAT32, SMB, etc.) that have no trash. Followed by fileOperations.delete.noTrashWarningRest in the same sentence.

@fileOperations.delete.noTrashWarningRes.description: Second half of the no-trash warning banner, following fileOperations.delete.noTrashWarningStrong. Tells the user the delete is permanent on this volume.

fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyMix: Some of your selection is online-only. Moving those to the Trash would download them first. In this case, Cmdr only offers to delete the entire selection. There’ll be no copies in the Trash, but cloud services usually keep their own trash for about 30 days. Click “Delete” if deletion is OK, otherwise cancel this dialog and either make all files available offline first, or deselect all online-only files.

@fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyMi.description: Warning banner in the delete dialog, shown when the person pressed the "move to trash" key over a selection where SOME items are online-only and the rest aren't. Online-only means the file lives in a cloud-storage folder (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, …) and the provider has evicted its contents to its own servers, leaving a placeholder on the Mac; "online-only" is Apple's Finder term, so prefer your platform's own existing wording for it. Four facts, all of which matter: (1) the Trash lives on the Mac, so putting an online-only file there would download it from the cloud service first; (2) because one gesture can't be half a trash and half a delete, Cmdr offers to delete the WHOLE selection permanently; (3) there will be NO copies in the macOS Trash afterwards, though the cloud service keeps its own deleted-files history (Dropbox keeps 30 days) to restore from — don't soften this into "it goes to the trash anyway", it does not; (4) two ways out, both real in Cmdr: make the files available offline (the provider's own download action, in Cmdr's right-click menu — don't name that menu item, its label comes from the provider), or deselect the online-only files (Cmdr badges them in the file pane). <strong> bolds "download them first" and "delete". “Delete” in quotes is the confirm button's own label: use the same word you translated fileOperations.delete.confirmDelete to. "Click" is deliberate even though Enter works too. "Trash" is the macOS Trash the Finder uses; the lowercase "their own trash" is the cloud service's, not Apple's.
@fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyMi.screenshotNote: The delete confirmation dialog, pictured here. Your string is one of its variants: a different item count, an archive or symlink warning, or the progress line it shows while scanning.

fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyAll: Everything you selected is online-only. Moving it to the Trash would download it first. In this case, Cmdr only offers to delete the entire selection. There’ll be no copies in the Trash, but cloud services usually keep their own trash for about 30 days. Click “Delete” if deletion is OK, otherwise cancel this dialog and make these files available offline first.

@fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyAl.description: The same warning banner as fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyMixedWarning (read its description for every term and fact), for the case where EVERY selected item is online-only. Keep the two in one voice; they differ in two places only: this one says the whole selection is online-only, and it offers just one way out, since "deselect the online-only files" would leave nothing selected.
@fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyAl.screenshotNote: The delete confirmation dialog, pictured here. Your string is one of its variants: a different item count, an archive or symlink warning, or the progress line it shows while scanning.

fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyHan: Your selection turned out to hold online-only content, so the button below now offers Delete. Read the note above, then press it again if that’s OK.

@fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyHa.description: Line that appears just above the confirm button in the delete dialog, after a press that Cmdr deliberately didn't act on. The person pressed "Move to trash", and while Cmdr was still counting a selected folder it found online-only content inside, which turns the whole thing into a permanent delete. Rather than run the one operation nothing can undo off a press that meant something else, the dialog stays open, changes its warning and its button, and says this. Tone: matter-of-fact, no apology, no blame. "Delete" names the confirm button's own label: use the same word you translated fileOperations.delete.confirmDelete to. "The note above" is the warning banner at the top of the same dialog. "Online-only" is Apple's Finder term for a file whose contents the cloud service has evicted to its servers.
@fileOperations.delete.cloudOnlineOnlyHa.screenshotNote: The delete confirmation dialog, pictured here. Your string is one of its variants: a different item count, an archive or symlink warning, or the progress line it shows while scanning.

fileOperations.delete.archiveWarningStro: There’s no trash inside an archive.

@fileOperations.delete.archiveWarningStr.description: Bold lead of a warning banner in the delete dialog, shown when deleting items from inside a zip archive (Cmdr browses zips like folders). Followed by fileOperations.delete.archiveWarningRest in the same sentence. "archive" = a zip file.
@fileOperations.delete.archiveWarningStr.screenshotNote: The delete confirmation dialog, pictured here. Your string is one of its variants: a different item count, an archive or symlink warning, or the progress line it shows while scanning.

fileOperations.delete.archiveWarningRest: These items will be removed from the zip for good.

@fileOperations.delete.archiveWarningRes.description: Second half of the archive delete warning banner, following fileOperations.delete.archiveWarningStrong. Tells the user the delete is permanent because a zip has no trash.
@fileOperations.delete.archiveWarningRes.screenshotNote: The delete confirmation dialog, pictured here. Your string is one of its variants: a different item count, an archive or symlink warning, or the progress line it shows while scanning.

@fileOperations.trash.undoAction.description: Button on the toast that appears right after files are moved to the trash. Pressing it puts every one of them back where it was. Short control label; the toast is narrow, so keep it to one or two words.

@fileOperations.trash.goToTrashAction.description: Button on the toast that appears right after files are moved to the trash. Pressing it opens the trash folder in the file pane, with the cursor on the item that was just moved there. "Trash" is the macOS Trash, so use whatever your platform calls the recoverable wastebasket. Short control label; the toast is narrow, so keep it to one or two words.

@fileOperations.trash.undoing.description: Replaces the toast while an undo is running, after the user pressed Undo on the trash toast. Putting files back can take a while on a slow or busy drive, so this is a progress state, not a result. Sentence case; the character at the end is an ellipsis. The files come back OUT of the Trash, so use the same verb as fileOperations.trash.undone.

@fileOperations.trash.undone.description: Result toast when an undo put every trashed item back where it came from. This is Finder's "Put Back": the items come back OUT of the Trash to their old folder, a different action from putting a file's old NAME back (askCmdr.renameUndo.undone), so use the verb your language uses for restoring from the Trash. Sentence case.

placeholders.countText: how many items came back, formatted for display (e.g. 1,234)
placeholders.count: the same number (drives the singular/plural form of the noun)

fileOperations.trash.undonePartial: Put back {restoredText} {restored, plural, one {file} other {files}}; {skippedText} {skipped, plural, one {item} other {items}} stayed in the trash.

@fileOperations.trash.undonePartial.description: Result toast when an undo could only put SOME items back. Cmdr never overwrites while undoing, so an item whose old spot is taken again, or that changed since, is deliberately left where it is. Say this as a considered choice, not as something going wrong. Sentence case. “Put back” is restoring from the Trash; use the same verb as fileOperations.trash.undone.

placeholders.restoredText: how many items came back, formatted for display (e.g. 1,234)
placeholders.restored: the same number (drives the singular/plural form of the noun)
placeholders.skippedText: how many items stayed in the trash, formatted for display (e.g. 12)
placeholders.skipped: the same number of items that stayed in the trash (drives the singular/plural form of the noun beside it, and any agreement your language needs in that clause)

fileOperations.trash.undoUnavailable: Nothing to put back. These items may already be back, or their drive isn’t connected.

@fileOperations.trash.undoUnavailable.description: Result toast when an undo had nothing to reverse: the items are already back, or the drive they belong on is no longer connected. Two sentences, both plain statements rather than a warning. Sentence case. “put back” here is restoring from the Trash, like fileOperations.trash.undone.

fileOperations.trash.undoGone: Nothing to put back: {count, plural, one {it’s} other {they’re}} no longer in the trash.

@fileOperations.trash.undoGone.description: Result toast when the user asked to undo a move to the trash, but the trash no longer holds any of those items (it was emptied, or they were deleted from it since), so nothing could come back. A plain statement, not a warning. Sentence case. “Put back” is restoring from the Trash, like fileOperations.trash.undone; use the same trash term as the rest of these toasts.

placeholders.count: how many items were no longer in the trash (drives the pronoun: one item or several)

fileOperations.trash.undoPartlyGone: {countText} {count, plural, one {item was} other {items were}} no longer in the trash.

@fileOperations.trash.undoPartlyGone.description: A second sentence added to an undo's result toast (after fileOperations.trash.undone or fileOperations.trash.undonePartial) when some of the trashed items couldn't come back because the trash no longer holds them (it was emptied, or they were deleted from it since). A plain statement, not a warning. Sentence case. Use the same trash term as the sentence before it.

placeholders.countText: how many items were no longer in the trash, formatted for display (e.g. 12)
placeholders.count: the same number (drives the singular/plural form of the noun and verb)

fileOperations.trash.noTrashHere: This drive doesn’t keep a trash.

@fileOperations.trash.noTrashHere.description: Toast shown when the user asks to go to the trash while standing on a drive that has none (a USB stick formatted FAT32, a network share). A statement of fact about the drive, not a problem with what the user did. Sentence case; the apostrophe is doubled for ICU and renders as one.

@fileOperations.delete.trashSwitch.description: Switch in the delete dialog, on by default. On moves items to the system trash (recoverable); off deletes them for good. Control label.

@fileOperations.delete.overflowMore.description: Trailing line of the delete dialog's file list when more items are selected than the list shows. Keep the leading ellipsis '…'.

placeholders.countText: how many extra items, formatted for display (e.g. 1,234)
placeholders.count: the same number of extra items (drives the singular/plural form of the noun)

@fileOperations.delete.scanFile.description: Unit noun shown after the live file tally in the delete dialog's scan stats (e.g. '123 files'). The number is rendered separately; this is only the noun.

placeholders.count: the file count (drives the singular/plural noun)

@fileOperations.delete.scanDir.description: Unit noun shown after the live folder tally in the delete dialog's scan stats (e.g. '4 folders'). The number is rendered separately.

placeholders.count: the folder count (drives the singular/plural noun)

@fileOperations.delete.confirmMoveToTras.description: Primary confirm button in the delete dialog when the trash option is selected. Control label.

@fileOperations.delete.titleCursorFile.description: Delete dialog title when deleting the single file the cursor is on (nothing multi-selected). 'under cursor' means the highlighted row.

@fileOperations.delete.titleCursorFolder.description: Delete dialog title when deleting the single folder the cursor is on (nothing multi-selected).

@fileOperations.delete.titleFallback.description: Delete dialog title used when there is nothing to count (empty selection). Just the verb.
@fileOperations.delete.titleFallback.screenshotNote: The delete confirmation dialog, pictured here. Your string is one of its variants: a different item count, an archive or symlink warning, or the progress line it shows while scanning.

@fileOperations.delete.titleSelected.description: Delete dialog title for a multi-item selection. {phrase} is the already-built count phrase (e.g. '3 selected files and 1 folder').

placeholders.phrase: the pre-rendered counts phrase, e.g. '3 selected files and 1 folder'

@fileOperations.delete.selectedFilesPart.description: The files part of the delete-dialog count phrase, e.g. '3 selected files'. Combined with the folders part by fileOperations.shared.andJoin.

placeholders.countText: how many files (plain number, not grouped)
placeholders.count: the same number of files (drives the singular/plural noun)

@fileOperations.delete.foldersPart.description: The folders part of the delete-dialog count phrase, e.g. '1 folder' or '2 folders'. Combined with the files part by fileOperations.shared.andJoin.

placeholders.countText: how many folders (plain number, not grouped)
placeholders.count: the same number of folders (drives the singular/plural noun)

fileOperations.delete.symlinkNoticeSingl: This item is a symlink. Only the link will be deleted, not its target.

@fileOperations.delete.symlinkNoticeSing.description: Notice in the delete dialog when the only selected item is a symbolic link. Reassures that the link is removed, not the file it points to. 'symlink'/'target' are filesystem terms.
@fileOperations.delete.symlinkNoticeSing.screenshotNote: The delete confirmation dialog, pictured here. Your string is one of its variants: a different item count, an archive or symlink warning, or the progress line it shows while scanning.

fileOperations.delete.symlinkNoticeMany: Your selection includes {countText} {count, plural, one {symlink} other {symlinks}}. Only the links themselves will be deleted, not their targets.

@fileOperations.delete.symlinkNoticeMany.description: Notice in the delete dialog when the selection contains one or more symbolic links among other items. Reassures that only the links are removed. 'symlink'/'target' are filesystem terms.

placeholders.countText: how many symlinks (plain number, not grouped)
placeholders.count: the same number of symlinks (drives the singular/plural noun)

@fileOperations.mkfile.notCreatedToast.description: Toast shown when a new file on a slow volume turns out NOT to have been created, after the person already closed the new-file dialog while it was still working.

placeholders.name: the file name the person typed, e.g. notes.txt
placeholders.reason: a full sentence saying why, already translated, e.g. 'There is already a file by this name in this folder.'

fileOperations.newEntry.stillCreating: Still creating “{name}”. The volume is slow to answer. Feel free to close this dialog, the creation will keep going, and there is no way to cancel it now.

@fileOperations.newEntry.stillCreating.description: Notice in the new-folder and new-file dialogs once the volume (a slow network share, a phone) has taken more than a couple of seconds to create the entry. It is still working and will most likely finish; the dialog closes by itself when it does. At this moment the dialog’s Cancel button turns into Close: closing the dialog does NOT stop the creation, which carries on in the background. There is no way to cancel it because the request is already with the volume, and the sentence tells the user so plainly.

placeholders.name: the folder or file name being created, e.g. photos

fileOperations.mkfile.title: New file

@fileOperations.mkfile.title.description: Title of the dialog that creates a new empty file (Shift+F4).

@fileOperations.mkfile.createIn.description: Subtitle of the new-file dialog naming the destination folder. <dir> wraps the folder name, which is styled (bold). Keep the sentence; only the folder name is highlighted.

placeholders.name: the destination folder's name

@fileOperations.mkfile.nameAria.description: Accessibility label for the new file's name text field (screen-reader only).

@fileOperations.mkfile.placeholder.description: Placeholder text inside the new-file name field, showing an example filename. 'notes.txt' is an example file name; translate 'Example' but keep a plausible example filename.

fileOperations.mkdir.title: New folder

@fileOperations.mkdir.title.description: Title of the dialog that creates a new folder (F7).

@fileOperations.mkdir.createIn.description: Subtitle of the new-folder dialog naming the parent folder. <dir> wraps the folder name, which is styled (bold). Keep the sentence; only the folder name is highlighted.

placeholders.name: the parent folder's name

@fileOperations.mkdir.nameAria.description: Accessibility label for the new folder's name text field (screen-reader only).

@fileOperations.mkdir.placeholder.description: Placeholder text inside the new-folder name field, showing an example folder name. 'my-project' is an example; translate 'Example' but keep a plausible example folder name.

@fileOperations.mkdir.notCreatedToast.description: Toast shown when a new folder on a slow volume turns out NOT to have been created, after the person already closed the new-folder dialog while it was still working.

placeholders.name: the folder name the person typed, e.g. photos
placeholders.reason: a full sentence saying why, already translated, e.g. 'There is already a folder by this name in this folder.'

@fileOperations.mkdir.aiSuggestionsAria.description: Accessibility label for the region listing AI-generated folder-name suggestions (screen-reader only). 'AI' is the common abbreviation.

@fileOperations.mkdir.aiSuggestionsHeade.description: Heading shown above the AI-generated folder-name suggestion chips in the new-folder dialog. 'AI' is the common abbreviation.

fileOperations.shared.conflictExistsFold: There is already a folder by this name in this folder.

@fileOperations.shared.conflictExistsFol.description: Inline validation error in the new-file and new-folder dialogs when the typed name matches an existing folder in the current directory.

fileOperations.shared.conflictExistsFile: There is already a file by this name in this folder.

@fileOperations.shared.conflictExistsFil.description: Inline validation error in the new-file and new-folder dialogs when the typed name matches an existing file in the current directory.

@fileOperations.shared.byteRate.description: Data-transfer speed shown next to a scan or copy/move bar, e.g. '1.2 MB/s'. <size> renders the formatted size (a widget, no inner text); '/s' means per second. Keep the per-second marker adjacent to the size. Its sibling fileOperations.shared.fileRate does the same job for the files-per-second rate; keep the two reading alike.

@fileOperations.shared.fileRate.description: How many files a second a scan or a copy/move is getting through, shown beside the bar and next to the transfer speed (fileOperations.shared.byteRate, its sibling — keep the two reading alike). '/s' means per second; keep that marker next to the number. {rateText} arrives ALREADY formatted for the locale, with the locale's own decimal mark and grouping ('0.4', '1,500'), so never re-format it or add digits to it. The plural is on the RATE, which is often a decimal below three ('0.4 files/s') and a whole number above it, so use your language's own plural categories rather than mirroring English's two: a language that always takes the singular after a number writes the same noun in every branch, and one with no plural forms needs only 'other'.

placeholders.rateText: the files-per-second rate, already formatted for display (e.g. 0.4 or 1,500)
placeholders.count: the same rate as a number (drives the singular/plural form of the noun)

@fileOperations.shared.andJoin.description: Joins two count parts into one phrase, e.g. '3 files' and '1 folder' become '3 files and 1 folder'. Used in delete and transfer dialog titles. Reorder the parts if your language needs it.

placeholders.a: the first part (the files count phrase)
placeholders.b: the second part (the folders count phrase)

@fileOperations.shared.scanningTooltip.description: Tooltip and screen-reader label for the spinner shown while the dialog counts the selected items (files, folders, total size).

@fileOperations.transferDialog.toggleCop.description: Label of the segmented-control option that sets the operation to copy. Short control label, sits next to Move.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.toggleMov.description: Label of the segmented-control option that sets the operation to move. Short control label, sits next to Copy.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.toggleCom.description: Label of the segmented-control option that sets the operation to compress (pack the selected files into a new zip). Short control label, sits next to Copy and Move.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.sourceGro.description: Heading over the group showing where the items come from: the full path of their current folder. Pairs with fileOperations.transferDialog.targetGroupTitle ("To").

@fileOperations.transferDialog.targetGro.description: Heading over the group that picks where the items go: the destination volume dropdown plus the destination path box. Pairs with fileOperations.transferDialog.sourceGroupTitle ("From").

@fileOperations.transferDialog.operation.description: Accessibility label for the Copy / Move / Compress segmented control at the top of the transfer dialog (screen-reader only). Names what the group chooses, not any one option.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.destVolum.description: Accessibility label for the dropdown that picks which volume (disk/device) the files go to (screen-reader only).

@fileOperations.transferDialog.destPathA.description: Accessibility label for the text field holding the destination folder path (screen-reader only).

@fileOperations.transferDialog.spaceInfo.description: Free-space line next to the destination-volume picker, e.g. '12 GB free of 500 GB'. Both values are already formatted sizes.

placeholders.total: total volume size, already formatted (e.g. 500 GB)

@fileOperations.transferDialog.spaceInfo.description: The line next to the destination-volume picker when that storage has no size limit, so there is no free figure to state: a cloud account with no quota, for example. Says what is stored and that nothing caps it, so the user knows the copy will fit. The value is an already-formatted size.

placeholders.used: how much is stored, already formatted (e.g. 64 MB)

@fileOperations.transferDialog.spaceInfo.screenshotNote: The copy/move dialog, pictured here. Your string replaces the free-space line next to the destination picker when the destination has no size limit, such as a cloud account with no quota.

fileOperations.transferDialog.smbNativeN: This share uses the system connection. Cancellation may be delayed. Use “Connect directly” in the volume picker for faster transfers and reliable cancel.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.smbNative.description: Note shown when the destination is an SMB share mounted by the operating system rather than connected directly by Cmdr. Warns that canceling a transfer may lag. Keep the quoted “Connect directly” matching that picker action's label.

fileOperations.transferDialog.targetWill: This folder doesn’t exist yet. Cmdr will create it during the copy.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.targetWil.description: Yellow inline warning beneath the destination path box in the Copy/Move dialog, shown when the typed destination folder doesn’t exist yet and the Copy action is selected. Reassures the user the folder will be made automatically. Active voice, friendly. Keep the product name 'Cmdr' as-is. There’s a separate '...Move' variant for the Move action.

fileOperations.transferDialog.renameByMo: Renaming this copies everything inside it on the server, so it runs as a move you can pause or cancel.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.renameByM.description: One-line note in the Move dialog when it opens to confirm a rename (the user pressed F2 on a big folder or file on cloud storage such as S3). There, a rename has no shortcut: every file gets copied to the new name and the originals deleted, so it runs as a regular move with progress. Reassures the user they can pause or cancel it. Friendly, active voice.

fileOperations.transferDialog.targetWill: This folder doesn’t exist yet. Cmdr will create it during the move.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.targetWil.description: Yellow inline warning beneath the destination path box in the Copy/Move dialog, shown when the typed destination folder doesn’t exist yet and the Move action is selected. Reassures the user the folder will be made automatically. Active voice, friendly. Keep the product name 'Cmdr' as-is. There’s a separate '...Copy' variant for the Copy action.

fileOperations.transferDialog.rootEchoWa: This place already starts in {rootFolder}, so this path leads to {resolvedPath}. Did you mean {strippedPath}?

@fileOperations.transferDialog.rootEchoW.description: Yellow inline warning beneath the destination path box in the Copy/Move/Compress dialog. The box takes paths relative to the chosen place (a server folder or phone storage), but the typed path starts with that place's own folder, so the folder appears twice in where the files go. Cmdr does what the box says; this explains the result and suggests the shorter path. A button beside it puts the shorter path in the box. Keep the three paths exactly as given.

placeholders.rootFolder: the folder the place starts in, as a path (e.g. /srv/data)
placeholders.resolvedPath: where the files go if the box stays as typed, as a path with the folder doubled (e.g. /srv/data/srv/data/photos)
placeholders.strippedPath: the typed path with the repeated folder taken off, which is probably what the user meant (e.g. /photos)

@fileOperations.transferDialog.rootEchoU.description: Small button inside the yellow warning beneath the destination path box (see fileOperations.transferDialog.rootEchoWarning). Pressing it replaces the typed path with the shorter one the warning suggests. A verb phrase for a button; keep it short.

fileOperations.transferDialog.destinatio: This folder is read-only, so nothing can go here.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.destinati.description: Red inline notice beneath the destination path box in the Copy/Move/Compress dialog, shown before confirming when the destination folder is on storage mounted read-only (a disk image, a write-protected card). Plain and factual, about the folder rather than the whole device.

fileOperations.transferDialog.destinatio: You don’t have permission to add files to this folder.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.destinati.description: Red inline notice beneath the destination path box in the Copy/Move/Compress dialog, shown before confirming when the user’s account isn’t allowed to add files to the destination folder. Plain and factual.

fileOperations.transferDialog.destinatio: This folder doesn’t accept new files.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.destinati.description: Red inline notice beneath the destination path box in the Copy/Move/Compress dialog, shown before confirming when the destination folder refuses new files and Cmdr can’t tell whether it’s read-only or a permission problem (for example the top-level folder of a phone connected over ADB). Keep it neutral: don’t claim read-only or a permission.

fileOperations.transferDialog.targetWill: A file with this name is already here. Cmdr will replace it.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.targetWil.description: Yellow inline warning beneath the destination path box in the Compress dialog, shown when a file with the typed archive name already exists at the destination. Confirming replaces it with the new zip. Active voice, friendly. Keep the product name 'Cmdr' as-is.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.scanFile.description: Unit noun after the live file tally in the transfer dialog's scan stats (e.g. '123 files'). The number is rendered separately.

placeholders.count: the file count (drives the singular/plural noun)

@fileOperations.transferDialog.scanDir.description: Unit noun after the live folder tally in the transfer dialog's scan stats (e.g. '4 folders'). The number is rendered separately.

placeholders.count: the folder count (drives the singular/plural noun)

fileOperations.transferDialog.hardlinkNo: <written></written> will be written. The source is <ondisk></ondisk> on disk – the extra is hardlinked files, which can’t stay linked across drives.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.hardlinkN.description: Note explaining why the bytes a copy will write exceed the source's on-disk size: hardlinked files become separate copies on another drive. <written> renders the to-be-written size and <ondisk> renders the source's on-disk size, both as inline size widgets (no inner text to translate). 'hardlinked' is a filesystem term. The dash is an en dash.

fileOperations.transferDialog.compressLe: Higher levels make a smaller zip but take longer to pack.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.compressL.description: Caption under the compression-level slider shown in the Compress mode of the transfer dialog. Explains the tradeoff: a higher level packs a smaller zip but is slower. "zip" is a file format; do not translate it.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.estimated.description: Label next to an approximate compressed-size figure shown in the Compress mode of the transfer dialog, e.g. "Estimated size ~ 42 MB". Keep it short. "zip" is a file format; do not translate it.

fileOperations.transferDialog.estimatedS: A rough guess at the packed zip. The real size may differ.

@fileOperations.transferDialog.estimated.description: Tooltip on the "Estimated size" label in the Compress dialog, clarifying the number is a quick approximation and the real packed size may differ. "zip" is a file format; do not translate it.

@fileOperations.s3Cost.line.description: One line in the Copy, Move, and Delete confirmation dialogs, shown once the size scan finishes when the source or destination is cloud storage (S3). fileOperations.transferProgress.lookAlik: These names look the same, but the server spells them differently. Overwrite replaces the one that’s there.

@fileOperations.transferProgress.lookAli.description: Quiet note in the conflict step of the copy/move progress dialog, under the name and folder of the item that's in the way. Shows only when the destination (usually a network share) holds an item whose name looks identical to the incoming one but is stored as different characters: for example 'café' written with a single 'é' character versus 'e' followed by a separate accent mark. On screen the two names are indistinguishable, so the note explains why the dialog asks about a name that seems to match. 'these names' means the incoming item's name and the existing item's name. 'the server' is the computer or network drive being copied to. 'spells them differently' means stores them as different character sequences; say it in plain words, not technical terms like Unicode or normalization. 'Overwrite' refers to the dialog's Overwrite button: use the same word as that button's translation (key fileOperations.transferProgress.conflictOverwrite). 'the one that's there' is the existing item, which Overwrite replaces while keeping its current name. Two short sentences. It explains; it isn't a warning (destructive clashes have a separate red warning).

fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.title: Roll this operation back?

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.title.description: Title of the dialog that appears when the user presses Rollback on a running or finished operation. "Roll back" means undoing the work done so far; the body under it says what that means for THIS operation, which is a delete for a copy and a journey home for a move.

fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.body: This deletes every file the operation has written so far, and any file it replaced won’t come back. Cmdr skips anything it isn’t sure about, so a few may stay behind.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.body.description: Body of the Rollback confirmation shown on a COPY (or a compress) that is still RUNNING. Three facts, all load-bearing: it removes everything written so far (not only the half-written file that a plain Cancel drops), a file that was overwritten during the operation is gone for good because no copy of the original was kept, and Cmdr leaves alone every file it can’t match against what it wrote, so the reversal can come out partial. Keep the last sentence parallel with the bodyStopAndMoveBack and bodyUndo* siblings, which make the same promise. Deliberately gives no file count: the running counter includes files the operation skipped, so a number here would be wrong. A running MOVE gets bodyStopAndMoveBack instead, because rolling one back deletes nothing.

fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.bodyStopA: This moves back everything the operation has moved so far, and any file it replaced won’t come back. Cmdr skips anything it isn’t sure about, so a few may stay where they are.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.bodyStop.description: Body of the Rollback confirmation shown on a MOVE (or a move to the trash) that is still RUNNING. The sibling of fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.body, which covers a running copy. The difference is the whole point: rolling back a move deletes NOTHING, it carries the files back where they came from, so keep the tone calm rather than a warning and never word it as a delete. Three facts, all load-bearing: everything moved SO FAR travels back (not only the file in flight, which is what a plain Cancel leaves), a file at the destination that this move overwrote is gone for good because no copy of it was kept, and Cmdr leaves alone every file it can’t match against what it moved, so the reversal can come out partial. Keep the last sentence parallel with its siblings. Deliberately gives no file count: the running counter includes files the operation skipped, so a number here would be wrong.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.titleFin.description: Title of the same dialog when the operation is already PARTLY rolled back, so pressing the button carries on from where the rollback stopped rather than starting a fresh one. The body under it is unchanged and still says what happens to the files. Sibling of fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.title, which covers the first time round.

fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.bodyUndoB: This deletes the files and folders the operation created. Cmdr skips anything it isn’t sure about, so a few may stay behind.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.bodyUndo.description: Body of the Rollback confirmation when the user undoes a FINISHED operation that created things: a copy, a new file, a new folder, or a compress. Two facts, both load-bearing: rolling back deletes what the operation made, and Cmdr leaves alone every file it can’t match against what it recorded (the user changed it since, it was never recorded, or the original a copy was made from is gone, so the copy is the only one left), so the reversal can come out partial. Sibling wordings cover undoing a move and undoing a rename; keep the second sentence parallel across all three.

fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.bodyUndoB: This moves the files back where they came from. Cmdr skips anything it isn’t sure about, so a few may stay where they are.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.bodyUndo.description: Body of the Rollback confirmation when the user undoes a FINISHED move, or a move to the trash. Nothing is deleted here, so keep the tone calm rather than a warning: the files travel back to where they started. Second sentence: Cmdr leaves alone every file it can’t match against what it recorded, so the reversal can come out partial. Keep it parallel with the sibling copy and rename wordings.

fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.bodyUndoB: This gives the files their old names back. Cmdr skips anything it isn’t sure about, so a few may keep the names they have now.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.bodyUndo.description: Body of the Rollback confirmation when the user undoes a FINISHED rename, whether one file or a batch of hundreds. Nothing moves and nothing is deleted; only the names change back, so keep the tone calm. Second sentence: Cmdr leaves alone every file it can’t match against what it recorded, so the reversal can come out partial. Keep it parallel with the sibling copy and move wordings.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.leaveAsI.description: Button that closes the Rollback confirmation without doing anything, shown when the user is undoing a FINISHED operation from their history. "It" is the operation: leave it standing as it is. The sibling button "Keep them" covers the other case, an operation still running, where "them" is the files it has written so far.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.keep.description: Button that closes the Rollback confirmation without doing anything: the operation carries on and the files it has written or moved stay where they are. "Them" is those files. Shown for an operation still RUNNING, whether a copy or a move; the sibling button "Leave it as is" covers undoing a finished one.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.rollBack.description: The confirming button on the Rollback confirmation: go ahead and undo the operation. The body above says what that does to the files, so this stays a plain verb and never names a delete. Styled as the destructive choice only in the two variants that really remove files. Matches the "Rollback" button that opened this dialog.

@fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.finishRo.description: The confirming button on the same dialog when the operation is already PARTLY rolled back: carry on from where the rollback stopped. Word it exactly like the "Finish rolling back" button in the Operation log that opened this dialog (operationLog.dialog.finishRollBack), so the two read as the same action.

fileOperations.cancelRollback.moveAlread: Cmdr stopped while removing the originals, but everything it moved is already at the destination and stays there. {count, plural, one {One original is still where it was.} other {{countText} originals are still where they were.}}

@fileOperations.cancelRollback.moveAlrea.description: Toast shown when the user stops a move between two different drives while Cmdr is on its last step: removing the originals, after every file has already arrived at the other drive. Two sentences with three jobs, and the order is the point, because it goes from what happened to why it is fine. (a) Cmdr was part-way through removing the originals when it stopped, so some of them are already gone: say this plainly, since the user needs to know it, but it must not read as a warning, because nothing went wrong. (b) The files themselves are whole at the other drive and are staying there: carrying them back would mean copying everything across the drives a second time, which Cmdr will not do, so this is a settled fact and never a promise to undo anything. (c) How many originals are still sitting in the folder the move started from. The ones already removed are not coming back, and no part of this may suggest otherwise. "Original" means the copy in the folder the move started from, as opposed to the one that has now arrived at the other drive; the app calls this phase "Removing the originals…" (fileOperations.transferProgress.titleRemovingOriginals), so use the same word for it as that key does. It covers both files and folders, and it counts the items the user picked, so one selected folder is one original however much is inside it. The second sentence sits inside the plural because the singular reads better without the number at all ("One original", not "1 original"); write each branch to read naturally in your language, and drop {countText} from any branch that doesn’t want it. Never use the words "error" or "failed". Sentence case.

placeholders.countText: how many originals are still in the folder the move started from, already formatted for display (e.g. 1,234)

@fileOperations.cancelRollback.leftBehin.description: Middle line of the toast after a cancelled copy or move whose undo left things behind. It sets the expectation BEFORE the reasons, so the user reads the leftovers as care rather than as something going wrong: Cmdr refuses to remove or move anything it can’t match against what it wrote. The lines under it (fileOperations.cancelRollback.reason.*) each name one reason and are shown as a bulleted list, which is why this line ends in a colon. It opens with the same verb as the Rollback confirmations (fileOperations.rollbackConfirm.body and its bodyUndo* siblings), which say Cmdr skips anything it isn’t sure about; keep the two matched in your language too. Sentence case; the apostrophe is doubled for ICU and renders as one.

@fileOperations.cancelRollback.recovered.description: One line in the toast after a cancelled copy or move when an Overwrite displaced an existing file or folder, but Cmdr could not put that original back under its old name because the incomplete replacement still occupies it. The original is safe under a sibling name ending in ‘ (recovered)’. Name BOTH full paths so the user can find it and knows which entry it came from. @fileOperations.transferTree.empty.description: Quiet placeholder in the live file tree of a copy/move/compress when the transfer holds no files or folders at all. Rare.

@fileOperations.transferTree.follow.description: Small button above the live file tree of a running copy/move/compress. It appears once the user has scrolled the tree or moved through it by keyboard, which stops the tree from scrolling along with the work. Pressing it makes the tree scroll back to the files being transferred right now and keep following them, like the follow mode of a log viewer. A verb, kept very short.

fileOperations.transferTree.followToolti: Scroll back to the files in progress, and keep following them

@fileOperations.transferTree.followToolt.description: Hover text of the Follow button above the live file tree of a running copy/move/compress (see fileOperations.transferTree.follow). Explains what the button does.

@fileOperations.transferTree.filesTotal.description: How many files a folder holds, in the small gray count text at the end of a folder’s row in the live file tree of a copy/move/compress. Shown before the folder’s files start and after they’re all done, for example “1,000 files”. A size may follow it after a middle dot. Screen readers hear it as one item of the row’s comma-separated description. Tight space: keep it short.

placeholders.countText: the number of files, already formatted for display (e.g. 1,000)
placeholders.count: the same number (drives the singular/plural form of the noun)

@fileOperations.transferTree.filesProgre.description: How far a folder’s files have got, in the small gray count text at the end of a folder’s row in the live file tree of a copy/move/compress, for example “312 / 1,000 files”. The slash reads as “out of”; keep it as a slash. A size like “1.2 / 4.0 GB” may follow after a middle dot. Screen readers hear it exactly as shown, as one item of the row’s comma-separated description (speech control finds the row by these words), so it has to read on its own. Tight space: keep it short.

placeholders.doneText: how many of the folder’s files are finished, already formatted (e.g. 312)
placeholders.totalText: how many files the folder holds, already formatted (e.g. 1,000)
placeholders.total: the same total number (drives the singular/plural form of the noun)

@fileOperations.transferTree.skippedCoun.description: How many files inside a folder were skipped (left out on purpose, for example because the user chose Skip when a file already existed), in the small gray count text of the folder’s row in the live file tree of a copy/move/compress, for example “3 skipped”. Follows the file count after a middle dot, and screen readers hear it as one item of a comma-separated list, so it has to read on its own. Word order is free: the number may come after the word. Tight space: keep it short.

placeholders.countText: the number of skipped files, already formatted (e.g. 3)
placeholders.count: the same number (drives the plural form and any agreement your language needs)

fileOperations.transferTree.failedCount: {count, plural, one {{countText} couldn’t finish} other {{countText} couldn’t finish}}

@fileOperations.transferTree.failedCount.description: How many files inside a folder couldn’t be transferred, in red in the count text of the folder’s row in the live file tree of a copy/move/compress, for example “1 couldn’t finish”. Follows the file count after a middle dot, and screen readers hear it as one item of a comma-separated list, so it has to read on its own. Gentle wording on purpose, the same as the queue’s status for an operation that stopped (queue.row.status): avoid the words error and failed. Word order is free: the number may come after the phrase. Tight space: keep it short.

placeholders.countText: the number of files that couldn’t be transferred, already formatted (e.g. 1)
placeholders.count: the same number (drives the plural form and any agreement your language needs)

@fileOperations.transferTree.state.waiti.description: State of a file or folder in the live file tree of a copy/move/compress that hasn’t started yet. Screen-reader only: read as the last item of the row’s comma-separated description, after the name and the counts the row shows.

@fileOperations.transferTree.state.copyi.description: State of a file or folder being copied right now, in the live file tree of a copy. Screen-reader only: read as the last item of the row’s comma-separated description, after the name and the counts the row shows. Siblings: fileOperations.transferTree.state.moving and fileOperations.transferTree.state.compressing for the other two operations.

@fileOperations.transferTree.state.movin.description: State of a file or folder being moved right now, in the live file tree of a move. Screen-reader only: read as the last item of the row’s comma-separated description, after the name and the counts the row shows.

@fileOperations.transferTree.state.compr.description: State of a file or folder being added to a new zip right now, in the live file tree of a compress. Screen-reader only: read as the last item of the row’s comma-separated description, after the name and the counts the row shows.

@fileOperations.transferTree.state.done.description: State of a file or folder that has finished transferring, in the live file tree of a copy/move/compress. The accessible name of the small checkmark at the end of its row, and one item of the row’s comma-separated screen-reader description. A row can be a file or a folder, so use a form that needs no agreement, or your language’s usual status form (masculine where that’s the convention).

@fileOperations.transferTree.state.skipp.description: State of a file or folder that was left out on purpose (for example the user chose Skip when it already existed at the destination), in the live file tree of a copy/move/compress. Shown as the gray count text of a skipped file’s row, as the accessible name of the small marker beside it, and in the row’s screen-reader description. A row can be a file or a folder, so use a form that needs no agreement, or your language’s usual status form (masculine where that’s the convention).

@fileOperations.transferTree.state.faile.description: State of a file or folder that couldn’t be transferred, in the live file tree of a copy/move/compress. The accessible name of the small red marker at the end of its row (the row itself shows the reason), and one item of the row’s screen-reader description. Gentle wording on purpose, the same as the queue’s status for an operation that stopped (queue.row.status): avoid the words error and failed. In a compress it means the file couldn’t be added to the zip, so a phrase that fits both is best. A row can be a file or a folder, so use a form that needs no agreement, or your language’s usual status form (masculine where that’s the convention).
